name: MemoryPack
workload: Serializing/deserializing POCOs and struct arrays via IBufferWriter<byte>, compared against System.Text.Json, protobuf-net, MessagePack-CSharp, and Orleans.Serialization
claimed_speedup: For standard objects, 10x faster and 2-5x faster than other binary serializers; for struct arrays, 50-200x faster than other serializers
tradeoffs: C#-specific zero-encoding binary format, not schema-based or cross-language; requires source-generator attributes and partial classes; only limited version tolerance by default
caveats: Numbers come from a first-party chart image, not a numeric table; hardware is stated but exact compiler/BenchmarkDotNet flags are not; benchmark code is public in the repo's sandbox/Benchmark project
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "serialization" language:C# --sort stars --limit 30, then README performance section

name: Nino
workload: Serialize/deserialize round-trip of a SimpleClass (ints, bools, GUIDs, dates, strings, arrays, lists, dictionaries) and a SimpleStruct, measured with BenchmarkDotNet
claimed_speedup: SimpleClass: 13.68x faster serialize / 5.17x faster deserialize than MessagePack (also 2.44x/1.90x faster than MemoryPack); SimpleStruct: 52.05x faster serialize than MessagePack (1.29x faster than MemoryPack)
hardware: Apple M1, 1 CPU, 8 logical and 8 physical cores, macOS Sequoia 15.1.1
tradeoffs: C#-only, source-generator based; smaller community/ecosystem than MessagePack-CSharp; Protobuf is not part of this specific comparison
caveats: Benchmark is on the project's own docs site (not an independent third party), though the benchmark project (Nino.Benchmark) is public in-repo and hardware/runtime are fully disclosed
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "serialization" language:C# --sort stars --limit 30, then https://nino.xgamedev.net/en/perf/micro

name: Nerdbank.MessagePack
workload: "SimplePoco" BenchmarkDotNet suite: round-trip serialize+deserialize of a simple object, in both map-encoded and array-encoded MessagePack modes
claimed_speedup: Array-encoded round-trip: 101.37 ns vs 120.51 ns for MessagePack-CSharp (~1.19x faster, derived from page data); map-encoded round-trip: 156.08 ns vs 148.36 ns (~5% slower than MessagePack-CSharp)
tradeoffs: Newer library than MessagePack-CSharp with smaller ecosystem; result is mixed rather than a clean win
caveats: Project's own docs explicitly state it and MessagePack-CSharp v3 (source-gen) are 'in the same range for steady-state throughput'; it only wins on the array-encoded workload and loses on map-encoded; no CPU model is disclosed
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "topic:serialization" language:C# --sort stars --limit 30, then https://aarnott.github.io/Nerdbank.MessagePack/docs/performance.html

name: msgspec
workload: MessagePack encode/decode of typical Python objects, compared against msgpack 1.0.7 and ormsgpack 1.4.1 on CPython 3.11
claimed_speedup: Described as "measurably faster than other Python MessagePack libraries like msgpack or ormsgpack"; struct operations are stated elsewhere as 5-60x faster than alternative libraries generally; exact MessagePack-specific multiplier is chart-only, not given as text
hardware: described only as "a ~2020 x86 Linux laptop", no exact CPU model
tradeoffs: Struct-based API rather than dict-based; MessagePack output is not a portable schema-enforced IDL the way Protobuf or Cap'n Proto schemas are
caveats: Numeric MessagePack-vs-msgpack speedup is only shown as an SVG chart, not stated as text; hardware description is vague (no CPU model)
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "fast serialization" language:Python --sort stars --limit 30, then https://msgspec.dev/benchmarks

name: flatty
workload: Serialize and deserialize an 11125-node tree structure
claimed_speedup: Serialize: 2.265 ms vs 85.178 ms for std/marshal (~37.6x faster, derived from page data); Deserialize: 2.643 ms vs 148.723 ms (~56.3x faster, derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Schemaless, requires 'flat' (non-cyclic, non-pointer) Nim object layouts for best performance; no cross-language support, no versioning
caveats: Baseline (Nim std/marshal) is not one of the four named category baselines (Protobuf/FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto/MessagePack), only Nim's own stdlib serializer; no hardware or compiler flags stated for the benchmark; benchmark code is public in tests/bench.nim
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "serialization" language:Nim --sort stars --limit 20, then README Speed section

name: s2s (ziglibs)
baseline: Protocol Buffers (also beats Cap'n Proto and Zig MessagePack implementations in the same suite)
workload: Serialize+deserialize round-trip across 5 shared benchmark payloads (document, event, message, strings, telemetry) generated from common suite IDLs, measured by an independent multi-language benchmark project (GLD.SerializerBenchmark)
claimed_speedup: ~1.1-2.0x faster than Arwalk/zig-protobuf across all 5 workloads; ~12.9-17.9x faster than the Cap'n Proto C++ runtime (via Zig C ABI) across all 5 workloads; ~1.4-2.2x faster than serde.zig's MessagePack backend on 4 of 5 workloads (all derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.x, release build (exact optimization flag not published on the methodology page)
tradeoffs: Zig-only, no IDL/schema, no versioning, not intended as a public interchange format (per author's own description); loses to FlatBuffers and to lalinsky/msgpack.zig on some of the 5 workloads even though it beats Protobuf/Cap'n Proto/serde.zig-msgpack on all of them
caveats: Evidence is a third-party benchmark suite (GLD.SerializerBenchmark), itself only 25 stars and first published 2026-09, not s2s's own repo; CPU model is not disclosed in the accessible docs/methodology pages, so this falls short of Tier A despite public code, stated compiler version, and stated statistical methodology
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "zig" "serialization" "benchmark" --limit 30 -> leo-gan/GLD.SerializerBenchmark, then dashboard/public/data/stats_zig_latest.json.gz
